title: Risk tolerance

objectives.text: Distinguish the ability to take risk from the willingness to take it.
Identify personal factors that shape risk tolerance.
Choose a portfolio risk level you can hold through a market fall.

explanation: Risk tolerance has two parts. Ability to take risk is financial: your income stability, emergency fund, dependants and how soon you need the money. Willingness to take risk is temperamental: how you would feel and behave if your portfolio fell 20% in a year. A plan needs both. Taking more risk than you can afford is dangerous, and taking more than you can tolerate usually ends in panic selling.

SEBI's investor material lists the risks that feed into this judgement, including market risk, inflation risk, liquidity risk and business risk. A useful way to test willingness is to ask what you would actually do after a sharp fall: sell, stop investing, or keep going. If the honest answer is sell, the portfolio is too aggressive for you, whatever a questionnaire says.

Risk tolerance is not a fixed personality label. It changes with your obligations, your job, your emergency fund and your experience. Reassess it when your circumstances change, and prefer a portfolio you can hold through a bad year over one that looks optimal only if markets behave. Diversification and a suitable horizon are the tools that make a chosen risk level survivable.

examples.title: Ability without willingness
examples.text: Aarav has a stable job, a six-month emergency fund and a 20-year horizon, so he can financially afford equity risk. But he checks his portfolio daily and sells whenever it falls 5%. His ability is high; his willingness is low. A smoother mix would serve him better than the most aggressive one.

examples.title: Willingness without ability
examples.text: Meera is comfortable with volatility and wants an all-equity portfolio. But she has no emergency fund, her income is irregular and she is repaying a loan. Her willingness is high; her ability is limited. Building a cushion first is the safer order of operations.

keyTakeaways: Ability to take risk is financial; willingness is behavioural.
A suitable plan respects both, not just the higher one.
Ask what you would actually do after a sharp fall.
Reassess risk tolerance when your job, dependants or emergency fund change.

quiz.question: What is the difference between ability and willingness to take risk?
options: Ability is financial capacity; willingness is how you would behave in a fall
They mean exactly the same thing
Ability is about age; willingness is about income
quiz.explanation: Ability depends on your finances, such as income stability and emergency savings. Willingness is behavioural: whether you can stay invested through losses.

quiz.question: Which factor most directly reduces your ability to take investment risk?
options: Having no emergency fund and irregular income
quiz.explanation: Without a cushion and with unpredictable income, a loss could force you to sell at the wrong time. That limits how much risk you can afford.

quiz.question: How should you choose a portfolio's risk level?
options: Pick the highest-return option regardless of falls
Pick the option a friend uses
Pick a level you can hold through a market fall and that fits your finances
quiz.explanation: A portfolio only works if you can stay with it. It must fit both your financial ability and your willingness to tolerate losses.

disclaimer: General financial education, not personalised advice. A financial adviser can help assess your circumstances, but the final decision is yours.
